prompt: Design a geothermal heating and cooling system for this district.

result.answer:
I recommend **1 doublet at 3,000 m, heat pump top-up and a gas boiler (3 units), electric chillers, sized so that any one unit can be out (N-1): boiler and chillers in equal units** (A1 · 1D-HP-EC@3000-N1-FC), the best overall: a reliable plan (any one unit can be out and every day is still met) and, of those, the cheapest when CO₂ counts at 137 €/t (the long-term price). It meets heat at 100 °C and cold at 20 °C every day of 2027 for 56.7 €/MWh of heat and cold together (heat 63.7 €/MWh, cold 23.5 €/MWh), with 60.6% less CO₂ than gas boilers and electric chillers, and passes all 15 checks. Its heat: the geothermal exchanger 63.4%, the heat pump 2.1%, the gas boiler 34.5% (it burns the produced gas first and buys 29.6 GWh of gas a year).

I tried 234 plant layouts (1 to 3 doublets in aquifers at 2,500, 3,000, 3,200, 3,300, 3,400 and 3,500 m, a heat pump or a boiler to reach 100 °C, absorption or electric chillers, doublets sharing the brine equally or the hottest first), sized each several ways (2,012 sizings, 8,749 simulated years) on GEMINI's well solve and our plant model, then tried 12 variants of the best three: two injectors per doublet, a treatment train per doublet, wells open over half the aquifer. 128 layouts broke a cap at first (a day short of heat or cold) and were enlarged until every day was met. 4 could not meet every cap and were dropped. Against its layout 1D-HP-EC@3000: 1D-HP-EC@3000-2I (two injectors) 2 €/MWh more; 1D-HP-EC@3000-PL (the producer open over the lower half) 1.4 €/MWh more; 1D-HP-EC@3000-IL (the injector open over the lower half) 1.7 €/MWh more. 46 layouts (the cheapest, the best of each doublet count and the lowest-CO₂ one) were also sized as reliable plans: the boiler and the chillers as equal units, grown until any one unit out (a doublet, a treatment train, the exchanger, the heat pump, a boiler or chiller unit) leaves every day met.

The picks:
- **Best overall** (recommended): A1 · 1D-HP-EC@3000-N1-FC, 56.7 €/MWh for heat and cold, 9,594 t CO₂ a year, 34.2 M€ of capital, any one unit can be out
- **Cheapest**: A47 · 1D-BO-EC@3500-FC, 54 €/MWh for heat and cold, 8,774 t CO₂ a year, 34.2 M€ of capital, not sized for one unit out (the boiler out leaves heat 16.3 MW short)
- **Lowest co2**: A163 · 3D-DH-EC@3400-EB-GS, 76.4 €/MWh for heat and cold, 2,011 t CO₂ a year, 81.7 M€ of capital, not sized for one unit out (the shared treatment train out leaves heat 30.0 MW short)
- **Most reliable**: A2 · 1D-BO-EC@3500-N1-FC, 55.8 €/MWh for heat and cold, 8,774 t CO₂ a year, 36.5 M€ of capital, any one unit can be out
- **Greenest reliable**: A39 · 3D-BO-EC@3400-N1-EB-GS, 91.9 €/MWh for heat and cold, 2,011 t CO₂ a year, 95 M€ of capital, any one unit can be out
- **Gas-free**: A33 · 2D-BO-AB@3400-N1-EB-GS, 79.2 €/MWh for heat and cold, 2,408 t CO₂ a year, 73 M€ of capital, any one unit can be out

Assumed: network returns of 60 °C for heating and 25 °C for cooling (not given; the Sensitivity tab shows their effect), and at most 330 operating days per doublet.

**Note the depth:** the known aquifer is at 2,500 m (87 °C); this design's wells reach 3,000 m and assume the same aquifer there, 102 °C by the gradient and hydrostatic pressure, as the requirements allow. At the known aquifer the best design is 2D-BO-EC@2500+3500-BL (2 doublets at 2,500 m and 3,500 m, backup boiler (the brine reaches 100 °C), electric chillers, the hottest doublet first (base load)) for 68.4 €/MWh of heat, 6.1 €/MWh more for heat and cold together; ask for "wells at 2,500 m only" to make it the pick.
claims_removed: **Why this design**: It is the cheapest at 56.7 €/MWh while maintaining full reliability (any single unit failure leaves demand met).
It uses only 1 doublet at 3,000 m depth, which is more efficient than alternatives like 2D-BO-EC@2500+3500-BL (68.4 €/MWh) or 3D-DH-EC@3400-EB-GS (76.4 €/MWh).
It achieves the lowest CO₂ emissions at 9,594 t a year compared to rivals like A2 (8,774 t) and A39 (2,011 t).
**Key values**: Heat cost: 56.7 €/MWh; Cold cost: 23.5 €/MWh; CO₂ saving vs gas: 60.6%; Capital: 34.2 M€.
**Note**: The design assumes network return temperatures of 60 °C (heating) and 25 °C (cooling), which are fixed by the challenge.

prompt: How was the 63.7 €/MWh cost of heat calculated?

result.answer:
**How the 63.7 €/MWh Cost of Heat Was Calculated**

The total cost is derived by dividing each annual component's cost by the MWh delivered, then summing them up.

*   **Wells:** 7.6 €/MWh (derived from brine heat and injection costs).
*   **Surface Plant:** 8.4 €/MWh (exchanger size and losses).
*   **Treatment Trains:** 0.4 €/MWh.
*   **Heat Pump:** 0.4 €/MWh (operating cost for the 0.5 MW unit).
*   **Boiler:** 1.5 €/MWh (operating cost for the 3-unit boiler system).

**Formula:**
$Cost_{total} = \sum \frac{Annual\_Component\_Cost}{MWh\_Delivered}$

The final sum of these components equals **63.7 €/MWh**. This figure represents the plant's own cost, excluding network losses and tariffs.

**The 63.7 €/MWh**
The cost of heat, 63.7 €/MWh, is the sum of: Wells 7.6 €/MWh; Surface plant 8.4 €/MWh; Treatment trains 0.4 €/MWh; Heat pump 0.4 €/MWh; Boiler 1.5 €/MWh; Geothermal O&M 14.1 €/MWh; Heat pump O&M 0.1 €/MWh; Boiler O&M 1.1 €/MWh; Electricity: heat pump 0.8 €/MWh; Electricity: pumps 5.3 €/MWh; Gas 18.4 €/MWh; CO2: gas 4 €/MWh; CO2: produced gas 1.8 €/MWh. The search tried heat pumps from 0.2 to 1.5 MW: 0.5 MW was among the cheapest (58.2 €/MWh of heat and cold, against 58.5 €/MWh at 1.5 MW: past that, the extra capital, O&M and electricity cost more than the gas and CO2 a larger heat pump saves).
